2.title: Fullness in Christ: Warnings Against Every Supplement
2.overview:
Now Paul names the danger. Teachers are offering the Colossians a “philosophy” that sounds wise: keep food laws and holy days, practise harsh self-denial, honour angels as mediators, and pursue visions. Its message is “Christ plus”. Paul answers in three steps. First, stay rooted in Christ, as you received him, because all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in him. Second, in him the whole fullness of God dwells bodily, and you are filled in him. You have already been circumcised, buried and raised with him; God made you alive, forgave all your sins, cancelled the record of debt by nailing it to the cross, and disarmed the spiritual powers, leading them in triumph.

Third, therefore let no one judge you over food or holy days, which were shadows of Christ, the substance. Let no one disqualify you with self-made severity, angel worship and visions: such people have let go of the Head, from whom the whole body grows. Rules like “Do not handle, do not taste, do not touch” look wise but have no power to stop the flesh. The cure for sin is not more rules but union with the risen Christ, which chapter 3 unfolds.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Rooted and Built Up in Him
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul wants them to know how hard he is struggling for them, for Laodicea, and for all who have never met him, that their hearts may be encouraged and united in love, so that they may have the full riches of assured understanding and know God’s mystery, which is Christ, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden. He says this so that no one deceives them with persuasive arguments. Though absent, he is with them in spirit and delights in their orderliness and firm faith. So, just as they received Christ Jesus as Lord, they should go on living in him, rooted, built up, strengthened in the faith they were taught, and overflowing with thankfulness.
verseByVerse.theology:
All the Treasures of Wisdom Hidden in Christ

Colossians 2:3 — “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” — is the epistemological foundation of the Reformed tradition’s approach to all knowledge. Cornelius Van Til’s presuppositionalism, Abraham Kuyper’s sphere sovereignty, Francis Schaeffer’s integrated Christian worldview: all are ultimately grounded in this text. All genuine wisdom and knowledge find their coherence and source in Christ. This does not mean that only Christians can know things; it means that all knowledge that is genuinely true is “thinking God’s thoughts after him,” participating (knowingly or not) in the structure of reality that Christ created and sustains. The Christian intellectual task is to follow wisdom wherever it leads, knowing that it leads ultimately to the one in whom all wisdom is hidden.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossian philosophy offered esoteric wisdom that seemed to go beyond what the gospel provided. Paul says: all the wisdom you are seeking is already hidden in Christ. You are not lacking wisdom; you have not been exploring deeply enough the one in whom wisdom dwells. Now: The Christian who turns to secular philosophy, psychology, or spirituality for the wisdom that Christ supposedly cannot provide has accepted the false teachers’ premise. All genuine wisdom, wherever it is found, is a trace of the one in whom all wisdom is hidden. The Christian engages with every source of wisdom while recognizing that Christ is its ultimate source and criterion.

verseByVerse.quote: For I want you to know how great a struggle I have for you and for those at Laodicea and for all who have not seen me face to face,
verseByVerse.commentary:
I want you to know how hard I am contending for you and for those at Laodicea, and for all who have not met me personally.

Strangers he loves. Paul had never been to Colossae; Epaphras planted it (1:7). He agonises for people he would not recognise in the street. A hireling cares for what the flock does for him; a shepherd cares for the flock (John 10:12–13).

Laodicea. Ten miles away, sharing the same danger (4:16). Later, the lukewarm church of Revelation 3:14–22.

Struggle. Agōn, the wrestler’s all-out effort, as in 1:29. In chains (4:18), he cannot visit. He struggles chiefly on his knees, like Epaphras, “always struggling on your behalf in his prayers” (4:12).

On a Tuesday. Somewhere an unseen believer may be praying for you by name. And this is what love looks like: labouring before God for a soul you may never meet. Choose a missionary or persecuted church and pray for them this week.
verseByVerse.note: Laodicea lay about 10 miles from Colossae.

verseByVerse.quote: that their hearts may be encouraged, being knit together in love, to reach all the riches of full assurance of understanding and the knowledge of God’s mystery, which is Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
My goal is that they may be encouraged in heart and united in love, so that they may have the full riches of complete understanding, and know the mystery of God, namely Christ.

What he asks. Not comfort or growth in numbers, but three deeper things.

Hearts encouraged. Paraklēthōsin: braced, given courage to stand against persuasive arguments (v. 4). The “heart” is the whole inner person.

Knit together in love. Woven into one body. The lone sheep is picked off; the knit flock stands. Heresy isolates and flatters the few; love weaves the whole body together, and understanding grows in that soil.

Full assurance. Plērophoria: settled certainty, resting on actually understanding the truth, not a leap in the dark.

The mystery is Christ. Not a secret doctrine but a Person (1:26–27). The false teachers dangled “knowledge”, “mystery” and “fullness” as prizes beyond Christ. Paul says they are Christ.

A textual note. This phrase has more manuscript variations than almost any in Paul: “of God, Christ”; “of God the Father of Christ”; “of God and the Father and of Christ” (KJV), and others. Scribes evidently tried to clarify an abrupt phrase. The short “of God, Christ” best explains the others and is likely original.

For worship. God’s desire is not that you be clever or initiated, but sure.

verseByVerse.quote: in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.

Treasures. What people dig, dive and travel the world to find. Knowledge (understanding God and reality) and wisdom (the skill of living in its light): all of it stored in Christ.

Hidden. Apokryphoi: not locked away from God’s people, but treasured up, as gold in a vault. Christ is God’s strongroom.

Their word, turned. The false teachers peddled “hidden” wisdom for the initiated, reached by climbing past Christ. All the truly hidden treasures are in Christ, who is “the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24, 30). You do not graduate from Christ; you go deeper into him.

Can unbelievers know truth? Yes. By common grace they discover much that is true, and Christians may learn from them. Paul means the wisdom that saves and makes sense of everything, found only in Christ. All truth is God’s truth, and coheres in him.

On a Tuesday. A man spends years chasing treasure schemes, then a lawyer tells him the deed to the richest mine in the country was made out in his name long ago. That is you and Christ (Matthew 13:44). You are not a second-class believer outside the vault.

verseByVerse.quote: I say this in order that no one may delude you with plausible arguments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I tell you this so that no one may deceive you by fine-sounding arguments.

Why the Christ-hymn. Paul reveals why he pressed Christ’s sufficiency so hard: a danger is circling.

The Colossian error. A blend of Jewish rule-keeping (food laws, holy days, perhaps circumcision, 2:11, 16), harsh self-denial, angel worship and claims to visions (2:18). Its method was not to deny Christ but to add to him.

Delude. Paralogizētai: to deceive by false reasoning, as a swindler reasons a man out of his money.

Plausible arguments. Pithanologia: persuasive speech. The peril is that error does not look false; it comes dressed as wisdom (v. 23).

The tell. The little word “plus”. Today: “Jesus, of course, but you also need this experience, this teacher’s system, these rules.” The guard: all the treasures are already in Christ (v. 3; 2 Corinthians 11:3).

On a Tuesday. When a teaching excites you, ask: does this make Christ bigger, or does it make him not quite enough?

verseByVerse.quote: For though I am absent in body, yet I am with you in spirit, rejoicing to see your good order and the firmness of your faith in Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For though I am absent from you in body, I am present with you in spirit, and I delight to see how disciplined you are and how firm your faith in Christ is.

With you in spirit. Not mystical projection but love that leaps distance (1 Corinthians 5:3), and the deeper bond of one Spirit in all believers.

Rejoicing in chains. Over the health of a church he has never seen (3 John 4; 1 Thessalonians 3:8).

Battle words. “Good order”, taxis: troops drawn up in ranks. “Firmness”, stereōma: a battle line that holds. The church is under attack, yet the line holds.

Praise before warning. He commends a line that is holding before reinforcing it.

Faith in Christ. Their firmness rests on its object. The line holds because the one it leans on cannot be moved (1 Corinthians 15:58).

On a Tuesday. Before you correct someone, name what is strong in them.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, as you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him, rooted and built up in him and established in the faith, just as you were taught, abounding in thanksgiving.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So then, just as you received Christ Jesus as Lord, continue to live your lives in him, rooted and built up in him, strengthened in the faith as you were taught, and overflowing with thankfulness.

Therefore. The hinge of the letter. Doctrine becomes duty.

Received Christ Jesus the Lord. Not a set of teachings but a Person, as Master. “Received” is the word for receiving a handed-down tradition (1 Corinthians 15:1–3).

So walk in him. The way you began is the way you go on. You came with empty hands, resting on Christ alone; keep walking that way. You do not move on from him; you go on in him: “Having begun by the Spirit, are you now being perfected by the flesh?” (Galatians 3:3).

Rooted and built up. Mixed metaphors, garden and building site (Ephesians 3:17; 1 Corinthians 3:9). “Rooted” is perfect tense: planted once for all. “Built up” is present: being built daily. Anchored and rising.

As you were taught. By Epaphras (1:7). The mark of truth is faithfulness to what was handed down, not novelty (Jude 3).

Abounding in thanksgiving. A heart overflowing with thanks for what it already has in Christ has no appetite for “something more”. Ingratitude is the crack where discontent enters, and discontent is the heretic’s foothold.

A textual note. Many later manuscripts read “abounding in it with thanksgiving” (KJV). The shorter text is earlier.

On a Tuesday. Israel ate bread from heaven every morning and grumbled the whole way. Count your mercies aloud today. You cannot grumble and give thanks in the same breath.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Do not let anyone take you captive through hollow, deceptive philosophy based on human tradition and the elemental forces of this world rather than on Christ. For in Christ the whole fullness of God lives in bodily form, and in him you have been filled, for he is head over every power and authority. In him you were circumcised, not by human hands, but by Christ, who put off your sinful nature. You were buried with him in baptism and raised with him through faith in God, who raised him from the dead. When you were dead in your sins and uncircumcised, God made you alive with Christ. He forgave all your sins, cancelled the charge of our legal debt, and took it away, nailing it to the cross. And having disarmed the powers and authorities, he made a public spectacle of them, triumphing over them by the cross.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Cancellation of the Debt and the Disarming of the Powers

Colossians 2:13–15 contains two of the most vivid metaphors for the atonement in the New Testament. First, the legal metaphor: the “record of debt” (cheirographon) that stood against us — the written bond of indebtedness, the document that recorded every sin and violation — has been cancelled, taken out of the way, nailed to the cross. The debt is not merely forgiven; the document is destroyed. Second, the military metaphor: the rulers and authorities who held humanity in their power through guilt and the law’s accusation have been “disarmed” and put to open shame — led in a triumphal procession like conquered enemies behind the victorious general. These two images together show what the cross accomplished: liberation from guilt (the debt cancelled) and liberation from spiritual bondage (the powers defeated).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossian philosophy appealed to the elemental spirits and cosmic powers as real and threatening forces that needed to be placated through ritual observance. Paul says: those powers have been disarmed. They are defeated enemies, paraded in public shame behind the triumphing Christ. You do not placate them; you stand on the victory that has already been won. Now: The Christian who lives in fear of spiritual powers — who approaches life with anxiety about demonic influence, spiritual attack, or cosmic forces working against them — needs to hear this: the powers have been disarmed. Christ has triumphed. The fear of powers that have been publicly defeated is not piety; it is a failure to reckon with the victory of the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: See to it that no one takes you captive by philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elemental spirits of the world, and not according to Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
See to it that no one takes you captive through hollow and deceptive philosophy, which depends on human tradition and the elemental spiritual forces of this world rather than on Christ.

See to it. A watchman’s cry: beware.

Takes you captive. Sylagōgōn: a slave-raider carrying off plunder. Seized physically, you would fight. Captured in the realm of ideas, the captive feels enlightened, not chained. Spiritual captivity wears the disguise of progress.

Philosophy. Not all careful thinking; Paul reasoned with philosophers at Athens (Acts 17:18–31). This particular system, hollow at the core.

Empty deceit. Promising fullness, delivering a void, while in Christ “you have been filled” (v. 10).

Human tradition. From men, not God: “you leave the commandment of God and hold to the tradition of men” (Mark 7:8).

Elemental spirits. Stoicheia: either the basic principles of religion, or, more likely, the spiritual powers thought to rule through calendar and stars (Galatians 4:3, 9). Both readings are held.

Not according to Christ. The hinge. Christ is the measuring rod. You need not master every cult; you need to know one thing surpassingly well.

Should Christians avoid philosophy? No. Study it, and every field, testing all by Christ and his word.

On a Tuesday. Bank tellers learn to spot forgeries by handling genuine notes constantly. Know Christ deeply, and what diminishes him will feel wrong at once (1 John 4:1).
verseByVerse.note: “Elemental spirits” may mean the basic principles of religion or the spiritual powers people believed ruled the world.

verseByVerse.quote: For in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For in Christ all the fullness of the Deity lives in bodily form.

For. The reason for v. 8: nothing can be added to Christ, because all of God is in him.

The whole fullness. Pan to plērōma: nothing left over, nothing elsewhere.

Of deity. Theotētos, the strongest word available: not divine qualities, but Godhood itself. Christ is not a creature filled with attributes; the complete divine nature is in him.

Dwells. Katoikei, present: permanent residence, even now in his exalted state.

Bodily. Sōmatikōs: in a real human body (John 1:14). All of God, in a body you could have stood beside.

Three blows. Against angels and elemental spirits: they have no fullness to offer. Against fullness spread thin across a chain of beings: it is concentrated in Christ. Against contempt for the body: God dwells bodily in Christ.

For worship. In Christ you do not have a fragment of God or a junior deputy. You have all of God there is (1:19; John 14:9).

verseByVerse.quote: and you have been filled in him, who is the head of all rule and authority.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And in Christ you have been brought to fullness. He is the head over every power and authority.

Fullness, filled. Plērōma in Christ (v. 9), peplērōmenoi in you: the same root. What is true of the Head overflows to the members.

Three things. Perfect tense: you have been filled and remain full. Passive: God did it. “In him”: by union, not attainment.

What it does not mean. Not sinless perfection, nor that you possess deity. You lack nothing for salvation, nothing for access to God, nothing for true completeness.

Head of all rule and authority. The powers the false teachers urged them to revere were created by Christ (1:16), will be disarmed by him (2:15), and are ruled by him. Not one outranks your Lord (Ephesians 1:21–22; Romans 8:38–39).

On a Tuesday. Like a man with a fortune in his account fretting that he is poor, you may feel like a second-rate Christian. The answer is not to earn more but to wake up to what is already yours.

verseByVerse.quote: In him also you were circumcised with a circumcision made without hands, by putting off the body of the flesh, by the circumcision of Christ, having been buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised with him through faith in the powerful working of God, who raised him from the dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In him you were also circumcised, in the putting off of the sinful nature, not with a circumcision done by human hands but with the circumcision done by Christ. You were buried with him in baptism, and also raised with him through your faith in the working of God, who raised him from the dead.

The true circumcision. The false teachers pressed the physical rite. Paul says the real thing, always pointed to, was a circumcised heart: “the LORD your God will circumcise your heart” (Deuteronomy 30:6; Romans 2:28–29), done by God, “without hands”.

The body of the flesh. Not a scrap of skin, but the whole old sinful self cut away.

The circumcision of Christ. Either the circumcision Christ performs, or Christ’s own “cutting off” in death, which the believer shares. Both fit.

Buried and raised. Baptism portrays the old life put in Christ’s grave and a new life raised (Romans 6:3–4). The ground of 3:1.

Through faith. Not the water by itself, but God’s power received by faith. Faith is the empty hand; God raises.

Does baptism replace circumcision? Christians who baptise infants argue that circumcision was given to Abraham’s infant sons and Paul links it here with baptism, so the sign belongs to believers’ children. Serious arguments. But Paul says the circumcision meant is “without hands”, inward, and they were raised “through faith”. He does not say baptism replaces circumcision; he says Christ’s inward circumcision is what circumcision pointed to, and baptism signs it for those who believe. The more likely reading is believers’ baptism.

Does baptism save? Roman Catholic and Lutheran Christians hold God gives new birth through it. Paul ties rising to faith. Baptism is God’s sign and seal and a public confession, not effective apart from faith. Burial and rising fit immersion most naturally.

A textual note. Later manuscripts read “the body of the sins of the flesh” (KJV). The shorter text is earlier.

For worship. You cannot improve on death and resurrection. You have been through the grave and out the other side in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: And you, who were dead in your trespasses and the uncircumcision of your flesh, God made alive together with him, having forgiven us all our trespasses, by canceling the record of debt that stood against us with its legal demands. This he set aside, nailing it to the cross.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When you were dead in your sins and in the uncircumcision of your flesh, God made you alive with Christ. He forgave us all our sins, having cancelled the charge of our legal debt, which stood against us and condemned us. He took it away, nailing it to the cross.

Dead. Not sick or struggling: spiritual corpses (Ephesians 2:1). Dead in trespasses, and outside the covenant as Gentiles, with hearts not yet renewed.

Made alive together. Synezōopoiēsen: resurrection language. You do not improve a corpse; you raise it. Not God helping those who help themselves, but life given to those who had none (Ephesians 2:5).

All. Charisamenos, from “grace”. All: past, present and future, the ones that haunt you at three in the morning, the ones never confessed to a soul (Psalm 103:12; Micah 7:19). Not cheap: Christ bore every one.

The record of debt. Cheirographon: a handwritten IOU signed by the debtor. God’s ledger of every command broken, “with its legal demands”, beyond all paying.

Cancelled. Exaleiphō: to wash the ink off the page, as though never written (Isaiah 43:25).

Nailed to the cross. Romans nailed a criminal’s charge above his head; over Jesus, “King of the Jews” (John 19:19). Paul says our charge-sheet was nailed there. How? Because our debt was laid on Jesus (Isaiah 53:5–6; Galatians 3:13). He took it into the grave, and it never came back out. The empty tomb is the receipt.

Why confess, then? As Judge, God has forgiven us once for all (Romans 8:1). As Father, he wants us to confess sins that spoil fellowship (Matthew 6:12; 1 John 1:9). We confess not to stay saved, but because we are his children.

The law nailed? Some take the record to be the Mosaic law itself. More likely it is our signed guilt before the law. Either way, the law cannot condemn those in Christ; love still keeps God’s commandments (Romans 13:8–10).

A textual note. Manuscripts vary between “made you alive” and “made us alive”, and “forgave you” and “forgave us”. Paul includes himself either way.
verseByVerse.note: The “record of debt” was a handwritten certificate of debt signed by the debtor; the charge against a crucified man was nailed above him.

verseByVerse.quote: He disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having disarmed the powers and authorities, he made a public spectacle of them, triumphing over them by the cross.

The powers. Not human kings but spiritual forces, “the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 6:12): created by Christ (1:16), ruled by him (2:10), and feared and courted by the false teachers (2:18). They held humanity through sin, through accusation, and through fear of death (Hebrews 2:14–15).

Disarmed. Stripped of weapons. Their great weapon was our guilt; the devil is “the accuser” (Revelation 12:10). Once the debt is cancelled (v. 14), the accuser has nothing to accuse with. The two verses are welded together.

The irony. The powers “crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2:8) and in that act were undone.

Triumphing. Thriambeusas, the Roman triumph: the victorious general in his chariot, enemy kings in chains behind him, paraded before jeering crowds. The cross, which looked like defeat, was the victory parade.

In him, or in it. The Greek can mean “in him” (Christ) or “in it” (the cross). Either way, the victory is at Calvary.

What it does not mean. Not that evil powers are imaginary or no longer active. They are real and beaten, like a fierce dog on a short chain, still barking and lunging, but unable to drag down one who belongs to the Victor (1 Peter 5:8; James 4:7).

On a Tuesday. You need not fear the dark or bargain with it. Stand in the finished victory (Romans 16:20).
verseByVerse.note: A Roman general celebrated victory by parading his captives through the streets.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: So do not let anyone judge you by what you eat or drink, or about a festival, a new moon or a Sabbath. These were a shadow of what was to come; the reality is found in Christ. Do not let anyone who delights in false humility and the worship of angels disqualify you. Such a person goes into detail about visions and is puffed up by an unspiritual mind, having lost connection with the Head, from whom the whole body, supported and held together, grows as God makes it grow. Since you died with Christ to the elemental forces of the world, why submit to rules like “Do not handle! Do not taste! Do not touch!”? These concern things that perish, and are based on human commands. Such rules look wise, with their self-imposed worship, false humility and harsh treatment of the body, but they have no value against the indulgence of the flesh.
verseByVerse.theology:
Shadow and Substance: The Old Covenant as Anticipation

Paul’s description of the Mosaic observances as “a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ” (v. 17) is the hermeneutical principle underlying all Reformed typological interpretation of the Old Testament. The ceremonial law — the festivals, the sabbaths, the food laws, the sacrificial system — was genuinely given by God and genuinely pointed forward to the reality that was coming. But it was always a shadow, not the substance; always anticipation, not fulfilment. The substance arrived in Christ. To return to the shadow when the substance is present is not faithfulness to the law; it is a failure to read what the law was always saying.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossian teachers were using Jewish observances as part of their syncretic system, insisting that the Colossians needed to keep certain days and food laws and festivals. Paul says: these were shadows pointing to Christ; Christ has come. Now: The same principle applies to any Christian movement that makes Old Testament ceremonial practices the standard of Christian spirituality. The principles of justice, love, and holiness that the ceremonial law expressed are fulfilled in Christ and applied by the Spirit. The specific ceremonies have been fulfilled in him who was their substance all along.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore let no one pass judgment on you in questions of food and drink, or with regard to a festival or a new moon or a Sabbath.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore do not let anyone judge you by what you eat or drink, or with regard to a religious festival, a New Moon celebration or a Sabbath day.

Therefore. Because you are filled in Christ, the debt cancelled, the powers disarmed.

The rules. Clean and unclean food and drink, and the sacred calendar: “festival, new moon, Sabbath” is the Old Testament’s standard summary of yearly, monthly and weekly holy days (1 Chronicles 23:31; Hosea 2:11).

Pass judgment. Condemning them for not keeping these, making them feel second-class.

What it does not mean. Not that such observances are sinful; a believer may hold convictions about days and food (Romans 14:5–6). But they may not be made the measure of anyone’s standing with God.

The weekly Sabbath? Many Reformed Christians, with the Westminster Confession, hold Paul means only Israel’s ceremonial sabbaths, and that the weekly Sabbath remains a creation ordinance (Genesis 2:3), now kept on the Lord’s Day. But Paul’s triad names yearly, monthly and weekly days together. The more likely reading is that the weekly Sabbath is included, a shadow fulfilled in Christ, whose rest we enter (Hebrews 4:9–10). Christians gather on the first day as a glad and ancient practice (Acts 20:7; Revelation 1:10), a privilege rather than a law binding the conscience.

The modern version. “A real Christian never touches a drink”; this diet or fast to be holy; must (or must not) keep Christmas or Lent; only this translation, these songs, this schooling. Wherever something Christ left free becomes a test of acceptance, that is the Colossian heresy in a Sunday suit.

Both ways. Do not let anyone make you feel second-rate, and do not judge a brother who differs (Romans 14:1–4; Galatians 5:1).

verseByVerse.quote: These are a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These are a shadow of the things that were to come; the reality, however, is found in Christ.

A shadow. The outline an object throws: its shape, none of its substance. The ceremonial law was a God-given shadow cast ahead of Christ (Hebrews 8:5; 10:1).

What each traced. The Passover lamb outlined the Lamb of God (1 Corinthians 5:7). The Day of Atonement, his once-for-all sacrifice. The Sabbath, the rest he gives (Matthew 11:28). The tabernacle, God dwelling with his people (John 1:14).

The substance. Literally “the body” (sōma): the solid body that threw the whole shadow is Christ. When your friend walks through the door, you do not keep staring at his silhouette on the wall.

What it does not mean. Not that the Old Testament is worthless. Shadows are real and God-given, and tell you something is coming. The moral law, which reflects God’s character, is not a shadow; the ceremonial law is.

For worship. Every feast and sacrifice was a finger tracing the shape of Jesus. Now the finger has found what it pointed at (Matthew 5:17; John 5:39).

verseByVerse.quote: Let no one disqualify you, insisting on asceticism and worship of angels, going on in detail about visions, puffed up without reason by his sensuous mind,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not let anyone who delights in false humility and the worship of angels disqualify you. Such a person goes into great detail about what they have seen; they are puffed up with idle notions by their unspiritual mind.

Disqualify. Katabrabeuō: an umpire ruling against a competitor and robbing him of the prize. The teachers set themselves up as judges of the Colossians’ faith.

Asceticism. Literally “delighting in humility”: self-imposed severity, harsh fasting, rough treatment of the body as a path to higher spirituality (v. 23). A performance of lowliness. Not an attack on genuine fasting, which Scripture commends, but on making bodily severity a badge of rank.

Worship of angels. Devotion to angels as mediators and guardians. It dethrones the one Mediator (1 Timothy 2:5). Angels refuse it: “You must not do that! … Worship God” (Revelation 19:10). Some read it as joining in the angels’ worship in visions; either way, it bypasses Christ.

Visions. Authority built on private experiences: “I have seen what you have not.” Spiritual one-upmanship.

A textual note. Later manuscripts read “intruding into those things which he hath not seen” (KJV), adding “not”. The earliest lack it: he goes on about what he has seen. The word embateuōn may be a term from initiation rites: “entering into” visions.

Puffed up by the flesh. The irony: the man who beats his body to escape the flesh is driven by the flesh’s craving for status. His “humility” is vanity in disguise.

On a Tuesday. Beware anyone who rates Christians by dramatic experiences, or slips angels or “spirit guides” between you and Christ.
verseByVerse.note: The false teaching seems to have mixed Jewish rules, strict self-denial and fascination with angels and visions.

verseByVerse.quote: and not holding fast to the Head, from whom the whole body, nourished and knit together through its joints and ligaments, grows with a growth that is from God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They have lost connection with the head, from whom the whole body, supported and held together by its ligaments and sinews, grows as God causes it to grow.

Not holding fast. The diagnosis of the whole heresy: for all his visions and disciplines, the false teacher has let go of Christ, the Head (1:18).

From whom. The whole body draws life from the Head alone. Fed and knit together through joints and ligaments that both link the parts and carry the supply. The growth “is from God” (Ephesians 4:15–16; 1 Corinthians 3:6–7).

A picture. Cut a branch from the vine and it withers (John 15:5). The false teachers offered a fancier life while cutting the branch from its only source.

Two lessons. Growth is not a technique to master but the fruit of staying joined to Jesus, through faith, the Word and prayer. And you do not grow alone: Christ’s life runs through the connections to other believers. A Christian was never meant to be a severed limb.

On a Tuesday. Stop hunting for life in programmes. Hold on to Christ, and stay connected to his people.

verseByVerse.quote: If with Christ you died to the elemental spirits of the world, why, as if you were still alive in the world, do you submit to regulations— “Do not handle, Do not taste, Do not touch” (referring to things that all perish as they are used)—according to human precepts and teachings? These have indeed an appearance of wisdom in promoting self-made religion and asceticism and severity to the body, but they are of no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since you died with Christ to the elemental spiritual forces of this world, why, as though you still belonged to the world, do you submit to its rules: “Do not handle! Do not taste! Do not touch!”? These rules, which have to do with things that are all destined to perish with use, are based on merely human commands and teachings. Such regulations indeed have an appearance of wisdom, with their self-imposed worship, their false humility and their harsh treatment of the body, but they lack any value in restraining sensual indulgence.

You died. Not a doubt but a fact. Joined to Christ’s death, you were released from the old regime; death dissolves every bond (Romans 7:1–6). Taking up its rules again is a freed slave walking back to pick up his old chains.

Do not handle, taste, touch. A religion of prohibitions, piling up: even the faintest contact banned.

Things that perish. Food is eaten and gone and cannot defile the soul (Mark 7:18–19).

Human precepts. “Teaching as doctrines the commandments of men” (Mark 7:7; Isaiah 29:13). Rules God never gave cannot bind a soul God has freed.

An appearance of wisdom. They look rigorous and holy. “Self-made religion” is ethelothrēskia, a word first found here: worship a man chooses rather than God commands. Self-will dressed as devotion.

No value. They fail at the one thing they promise. Starve the body and the flesh grows fat on pride. Rules can trim behaviour but cannot change a heart, and may even inflame what they forbid (Romans 7:5–8).

Is fasting pointless, then? No. Jesus expected his disciples to fast (Matthew 6:16–18); Paul disciplined his body (1 Corinthians 9:27). What Paul condemns is rules imposed as the way to holiness or acceptance.

On a Tuesday. Cutting weeds at ground level makes the garden look tidy for a day; the roots live. Only Christ digs out the root (Romans 8:13; Galatians 5:16). Chapter 3 shows how.
